summary: Defines MZAP, a protocol for discovering the multicast administrative scope zones relevant at a particular location. It was a standards-track document, and its status is now historic.

plainLanguage.summary: MZAP lets devices learn which administratively scoped multicast zones are relevant where they are connected. Its messages also help routers detect several kinds of boundary misconfiguration.

questions: how to discover multicast scope zones
how does mzap announce multicast zones
how does mzap detect a leaking boundary
subtitle: How routers announce multicast scope zones and detect common boundary configuration errors.

tldr.problem: Hosts and applications need to know which administratively scoped multicast zones are local. Misconfigured boundaries can also make a zone leak or fail to form a connected region.
tldr.mechanism: Zone Boundary Routers send announcements and related messages. Hosts can learn zone details, while routers compare messages and routing information to detect configuration problems.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2776 is Historic. Its specification defines zone discovery, nesting information and router diagnostics for administratively scoped multicast.

today: RFC 2776 is Historic. The RFC defines how MZAP announces multicast scope zones and detects common router misconfigurations.

sections.title: Why Discover Multicast Zones
sections.content:
Administrators can divide multicast addresses into scopes and configure router boundaries to keep packets in a chosen part of a network. A scope zone is a region of the network inside such boundaries. Different regions may reuse the same address range.

The RFC identifies two difficulties: applications cannot discover the zones that apply to them, and misconfigured boundaries are hard to notice. MZAP addresses both by announcing zone information and giving routers ways to detect common errors.
sections.plainLanguage: A multicast scope limits where packets can travel. MZAP helps a device learn the scopes around it and helps routers find boundary mistakes.

sections.title: Zone Boundaries and Zone IDs
sections.content:
A Zone Boundary Router (ZBR) has a configured boundary for a multicast scope on one or more interfaces. Each interface with an administrative scope boundary must also have a Local Scope boundary. A Zone ID is the lowest IP address used by an active ZBR in that zone to send MZAP messages into it.

A host can listen for announcements, but the RFC describes a Multicast Address Allocation Server as the usual source for applications. The server listens to MZAP and can provide local scope information to clients.
sections.plainLanguage: A Zone Boundary Router is a router configured to limit a multicast scope. The Zone ID identifies a zone using the lowest address of an active boundary router.

sections.title: Announcements and Zone Nesting
sections.content:
A ZBR periodically sends a Zone Announcement Message (ZAM) for each non-local, non-link-local scope for which it is a boundary. The message carries the address range, Zone ID and optional names. Routers relay announcements across Local Scope boundaries, adding path information to reduce repeated forwarding.

Not-Inside Messages (NIMs) state that one zone is not inside another. A listener can infer nesting only after it has received announcements for both zones and has not received contrary NIM information for the required hold time.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers announce a zone's range and name, then relay that information into nearby Local Scope areas. A NIM says that one zone is not inside another; listeners use these messages to work out nesting.

sections.title: Detecting Boundary Errors
sections.content:
Zone Convexity Messages (ZCMs) list boundary routers that a sender can hear. A router can detect a non-convex zone if a listed router is unreachable through the zone or its messages stop arriving. A ZAM arriving from outside its scope can indicate a leaking boundary; a Zone Limit Exceeded message can reveal a leak that reaches distant Local Scope zones.

Routers can also compare a received zone's address range and name with local configuration. An overlapping but different range, or a different name for the same scope and language, indicates a conflict. The RFC says a router should alert an administrator when it detects an error.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers compare reports to find zones with gaps, leaking packets or conflicting settings. MZAP reports the problem to the router; a network administrator must determine how to fix it.

sections.title: Message Format and Security
sections.content:
MZAP messages use UDP port 2106 and an IP TTL or IPv6 Hop Limit of 255. The common header identifies the version, packet type, address family and zone names, and carries the origin address, Zone ID and range. The four types are ZAM, ZLE, ZCM and NIM.

The RFC says unauthenticated messages can mislead listeners about a zone's existence or nesting. It describes IPsec Authentication Header as a way to authenticate messages and gives additional checks for address-allocation servers receiving ZAMs.
sections.plainLanguage: MZAP sends four message types over UDP. Unauthenticated announcements can give false scope information, so the RFC describes authentication checks for routers and allocation servers.
